record.paper_title: Major Unsolved Problems in Space Plasma Physics
record.original_question: For solar flares and coronal mass ejections, what is the geometry of coronal mass ejections and how do they exit the solar corona and evolve into the solar wind? For type II solar radio bursts, where relative to the collisionless shock wave are the electrons accelerated, and where are the fundamental and second-harmonic radio emissions generated?

evidence.quote: One problem at the top of most lists is solar flares and coronal mass ejections (CMEs).
exactly what their geometry is and how they exit from the corona and evolve into the solar wind are still subjects of intense research.
Where in relation to the collisionless shock wave are the electrons accelerated? Where are the fundamental and second harmonic radiation generated?

artifact.category_tag: solar coronal mass ejections and type II radio bursts
artifact.self_contained_problem:
Consider the magnetohydrodynamic (MHD) description of the solar corona, in which the plasma is governed by the ideal/resistive MHD equations coupled to Maxwell's equations, together with a kinetic (Vlasov–Maxwell) description of suprathermal electrons near collisionless shock waves. A coronal mass ejection (CME) is a large-scale eruption of magnetized plasma that detaches from the low corona and propagates into the heliosphere, eventually merging with the ambient solar wind (a continuously expanding plasma outflow from the Sun). A type II solar radio burst is slowly drifting radio emission, observed at a fundamental frequency near the local electron plasma frequency f_p = (1/2π)√(n_e e²/ε₀ m_e) and at its second harmonic 2f_p, produced in association with a collisionless MHD shock wave driven by a CME or flare.

Address the following:

(a) Geometry and evolution of CMEs. Provide a quantitative model of the three-dimensional magnetic and density structure of a coronal mass ejection (e.g., as a flux rope, spheromak, or other topology) and determine, from first-principles MHD, the mechanism and trajectory by which such a structure detaches from the closed coronal magnetic field, escapes the corona, and evolves dynamically into a self-similar or steady-state structure embedded in the ambient solar wind.

(b) Electron acceleration in type II bursts. For a collisionless fast-mode shock with upstream magnetic field B, density n_e, and shock normal angle θ_Bn, determine the spatial region — upstream foreshock, shock ramp, or downstream — in which the suprathermal electron beams responsible for type II radio emission are accelerated, and characterize the acceleration mechanism (e.g., shock drift acceleration, diffusive shock acceleration, or stochastic acceleration).

(c) Radio emission sites. Within the same shock geometry, determine the spatial locations at which the fundamental (near f_p) and second-harmonic (near 2f_p) electromagnetic emissions are generated via plasma-emission processes (Langmuir-wave excitation followed by linear mode conversion and/or nonlinear three-wave coupling L + L' → T at 2f_p and L + S → T at f_p), and predict the resulting source separation and frequency-band ratio.
artifact.status_search_result: CME initiation, three-dimensional geometry, and coupling to the solar wind remain active areas of research, with no consensus model; likewise, the precise acceleration site of energetic electrons relative to CME-driven shocks and the location of fundamental vs. harmonic plasma emission in type II bursts are still debated in current heliophysics literature (recent reviews and Parker Solar Probe / Solar Orbiter studies continue to investigate these questions).

status_evidence.title: Coronal Mass Ejections: Models and Their Observational Basis
status_evidence.snippet: Despite decades of study, the initiation mechanism and three-dimensional structure of CMEs remain open questions.
status_evidence.claim: CME geometry and eruption mechanism are unsolved.

status_evidence.title: Type II Solar Radio Bursts: Theory and Space Weather Implications
status_evidence.snippet: The exact location of electron acceleration at CME-driven shocks and the sites of fundamental and harmonic emission remain unresolved.
status_evidence.claim: Acceleration site and emission locations in type II bursts are open problems.
